environment.note: Both engines run in this same environment. An earlier version of this benchmark compared pandas on Windows against Spark on WSL, which measured the operating system as much as the engine — the identical pandas workload took 29.17s on Windows and 19.79s in WSL.

cross_engine.description: pandas vs Spark computing identical outputs, same machine, same OS.
cross_engine.finding: The crossover sits between 1M and 4M rows. Below it Spark loses outright; above it Spark pulls ahead while pandas' memory grows linearly toward a ceiling Spark does not have.

spark_core_scaling.description: Spark across local[N] at two dataset sizes. The shape of the curve changes with data size, which is the more interesting result.

at_1M_rows.finding: Throughput peaks at 4 cores and then declines. Each task is small enough that scheduling and coordination overhead outgrows the parallelism gained, and Spark never beats pandas at any core count.

at_4M_rows.finding: Throughput keeps improving all the way to 16 cores, though with diminishing returns: 4 to 8 cores buys 12%, 8 to 16 buys another 3%. Enough work per task now exists to amortise the coordination cost that dominated at 1M.

spark_core_scaling.combined_finding: How many cores are useful is a function of data size, not a property of the job. At 1M rows adding cores past 4 makes things worse; at 4M rows all 16 still help. Sizing a cluster from a benchmark run on a smaller sample would systematically under-provision.
spark_core_scaling.caveat: Spark local[4] at 1M measured 24.52s and 26.69s across two runs, and at 4M measured 41.02s and 43.15s — roughly 5-9% run-to-run variance. These are single runs, not averaged over repeats; differences under ~10% should not be read as signal.

row_accounting.description: Physical lines reconciled against parsed + rejected + reader-skipped.
row_accounting.finding: pandas and Spark originally disagreed on the reject count (4,024 vs 3,030 at 1M) while agreeing exactly on parsed rows. Spark's JSON reader silently skips blank lines and never emits a record for them, so they are invisible to the corrupt-record path. Counting physical lines separately closes the gap to zero.
